mutually-exclusive-s2.title: Events for one roll of a die
mutually-exclusive-s2.text: A fair die is rolled once. Event V: the roll is even (2, 4, 6). Event F: the roll is a 5. Event G: the roll is greater than 3 (4, 5, 6).

items.q: What is $P(\text{senior} \cap \text{plays a sport})$, the probability that the student is a senior and plays a sport?

why.correct: The joint event is one cell: 15 seniors play a sport. Out of 200 equally likely students, $\frac{15}{200} = 0.075$.

mistakes.why: That divides by the 50 seniors. The student is chosen from all 200, so divide by 200.
That divides by the 75 students who play a sport. Divide by all 200.

items.q: Are the events "the student is a freshman" and "the student is a senior" mutually exclusive?

why.correct: No student is in two classes, so the joint event has no outcomes: $P(\text{freshman} \cap \text{senior}) = 0$.
options: Equal probabilities have nothing to do with being mutually exclusive.
Sharing a third feature does not put a student in both classes.
Together they cover only 100 students; and covering everything is not the test.
Right: they cannot happen together.
No: each event has the same probability, 0.25
No: some freshmen and some seniors play a sport
Yes: together they make up the whole school of 200 students
Yes: no student is both a freshman and a senior

items.q: Are "the student is a junior" and "the student plays a sport" mutually exclusive?

why.correct: 18 students are juniors who play a sport, so $P(\text{junior} \cap \text{plays a sport}) = \frac{18}{200} = 0.09$, not 0. The events can happen together.
options: Right: the joint probability is not 0.
Mutually exclusive means no overlap at all, not "mostly separate".
Events on different variables can happen together, as these do.
The size of each probability is not the test; the joint probability is.
No, because 18 students are juniors on a team, so the joint probability is 0.09
Yes, because more juniors do not play a sport (32) than play one (18)
Yes, because class and sport are two different variables
No, because both events have probability above 0.2

items.q: What is the probability that the student is a freshman or a senior?

why.correct: The two events are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add: $\frac{50}{200} + \frac{50}{200} = 0.5$. No student is counted twice.

mistakes.why: That is the probability of just one of the classes. "Freshman or senior" includes both groups, 100 students.

items.q: Write an expression for $P(\text{sophomore} \cap \text{plays a sport})$.

why.correct: The joint event is the cell for sophomores who play a sport, 22 students, over all 200: $\frac{22}{200} = 0.11$.

mistakes.why: That divides by the 50 sophomores. The student comes from all 200.
That divides by the 75 students on teams. Use all 200.

items.q: Which pair of events is mutually exclusive?

why.correct: V is 2, 4, 6 and F is 5: no outcome is in both. V and G share 4 and 6; F and G share 5.
options: They share 4 and 6, so they can happen together.
A 5 is greater than 3, so F and G happen together on a 5.
A 6 is in G, so they overlap.
Right: an even roll can never be a 5.
V and G
F and G
G and "the roll is 6"
V and F

items.q: What is $P(V \cap G)$, the probability that the roll is even and greater than 3?

why.correct: The outcomes in both events are 4 and 6. Two of six equally likely outcomes: $\frac{2}{6} \approx 0.333$.

mistakes.why: That counts outcomes in either event (2, 4, 5, 6). The joint event needs both: even AND greater than 3.
That multiplies the two probabilities. List the outcomes in both events instead: 4 and 6.

items.q: What is the probability that the roll is even or a 5?

why.correct: V and F are mutually exclusive, so the probabilities add: $\frac{3}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{6}$ (the rolls 2, 4, 5, 6).
options: That is the even rolls alone, without the 5.
Right: 2, 4, 5 and 6.
That is the 5 alone.
That multiplies the probabilities, which does not give the chance of one or the other.

items.q: A student finds the probability that the roll is even or greater than 3 as $\frac{3}{6} + \frac{3}{6} = 1$. What went wrong?

why.correct: V and G are not mutually exclusive: 4 and 6 are in both, so adding counts them twice. Listing the outcomes, 2, 4, 5, 6, gives $\frac{4}{6}$.
options: A probability of 1 would mean a 1 or a 3 could never be rolled, which is false.
Multiplying does not give the chance of one event or the other.
Right: adding works only for mutually exclusive events.
The fractions already use 6 as the denominator.
Nothing went wrong, since each event has probability one half
The student should have multiplied the probabilities to get one fourth
The events overlap at 4 and 6, so those rolls were counted twice
The die has 6 faces, so the answer should have been divided by 6

items.q: Two events are mutually exclusive when

why.correct: Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events have no outcomes in common, so they cannot happen together and their joint probability is 0.
options: That describes an event and its complement, one special case.
Equal chances are a different idea.
That is about how events affect each other, not whether they overlap.
Right: no shared outcomes.
their probabilities add to 1 and one of them is sure to happen
they have the same probability of happening on any one trial
one of them makes the other more likely to happen on the next trial
they cannot happen on the same trial, so their joint probability is 0

items.q: An adult is chosen at random. Which pair of events is mutually exclusive?

why.correct: A person has one blood type, so "type A blood" and "type O blood" cannot both happen. The other pairs can happen together.
options: Right: a person has exactly one blood type.
Many people own both a dog and a cat.
Many teenagers have a license.
Someone can be born on a Monday in May.
Has type A blood; has type O blood
Owns a dog; owns a cat
Is under 20 years old; has a driver's license
Was born in May; was born on a Monday

items.q: At a diner, each customer orders exactly one main course. The probability that a customer orders a salad is 0.30 and that a customer orders a burger is 0.45. What is the probability that the next customer orders a salad or a burger?

why.correct: One main course each means a customer cannot order both, so the events are mutually exclusive and the probabilities add: $0.30 + 0.45 = 0.75$.

mistakes.why: That multiplies the probabilities. For "one or the other" with no overlap, add them.
That is the probability of neither, $1 - 0.75$.

items.q: Event H has probability 0.6 and event K has probability 0.5. Can H and K be mutually exclusive?

why.correct: If they could not happen together, the probability of H or K would be $0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1$, more than 1, which is impossible. So H and K must overlap.
options: Different probabilities do not separate events.
Probabilities of mutually exclusive events add to at most 1.
Right: no probability can exceed 1.
The numbers alone settle it: 0.6 + 0.5 is more than 1.
Yes: any two events with different probabilities are mutually exclusive
Yes: mutually exclusive events have probabilities that add to more than 1
No: then the chance of one or the other would be 1.1, more than 1
It depends on whether H makes K more likely to happen

items.q: In a survey of a school, 12% of students both walk to school on some days and ride a bike on other days. Are "walks some days" and "bikes some days" mutually exclusive for a randomly chosen student?

why.correct: The joint probability is 0.12, not 0, so the events can happen together: they are not mutually exclusive.
options: The events are about "some days", and 12% of students do both.
Small is not zero; any overlap means not mutually exclusive.
Being similar is not the test; sharing outcomes is.
Right: mutually exclusive means a joint probability of 0.
Yes, because a student is unable to walk and bike on the same day
Yes, because 12% is a small percent of the students
No, because walking and biking are both ways to get to school
No, because the probability of both is 0.12, not 0

items.q: A company has 400 workers. 90 work night shifts, 150 are part-time, and 64 are part-time workers on night shifts. A worker is chosen at random. Find $P(\text{night shift} \cap \text{part-time})$.

why.correct: The joint event is the 64 workers who are both, out of 400: $\frac{64}{400} = 0.16$.

mistakes.why: That divides by the 90 night workers. The worker is chosen from all 400.
That adds the two groups. The joint event is only the 64 workers in both.

items.q: Events R and T are mutually exclusive. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Mutually exclusive means no shared outcomes: $P(R \cap T) = 0$, and if R happens, T does not. Their probabilities need not add to 1 or be equal.
options: Right: the joint event has no outcomes.
Right: they cannot happen together.
That holds for an event and its complement, not for every pair of mutually exclusive events.
Complements are mutually exclusive, but mutually exclusive events may leave other outcomes.
Mutually exclusive events can have any probabilities that add to 1 or less.
$P(R \cap T) = 0$
If R happens on a trial, T does not happen on that trial
R and T are complements of each other
